explanations.explanation: Land it is, baker. On the fourteenth night, about midnight, the sailors sensed they were approaching land. I think those sailors perked up faster than I do when the oven timer dings. After fourteen nights of being driven across the sea, that's news.

After two weeks of open water, I'd be squinting for another ship too, friend. But the text says the sailors sensed they were approaching land. The next verse has them checking the water depth, and you don't do that for a passing ship. Land was the answer.

A giant wave sounds fair after fourteen nights of being driven across the sea, I'll give you that. But the text says that about midnight the sailors sensed they were approaching land. Right after that, they took soundings and found the water was twenty fathoms deep.

Fifteen is right. The first reading was twenty fathoms, then they went a little farther and got fifteen. Right after that, fearing they would run aground on the rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern.

Thirty is a bigger number than twenty, baker, and that's not what the second reading showed. The sailors went from twenty fathoms to fifteen. Right after that, fearing they would run aground on the rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern.

Forty would be a big jump into deep water, and these sailors saw the opposite. The text says the first reading was twenty fathoms, and the next one was fifteen. Numbers going down, friend, and the sailors did not like where that was heading.

True. Fearing they would run aground on the rocks, the sailors dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for daybreak. Notice they put the anchors down first and asked for morning second. Four anchors in the dark and a prayer for light, and I'd have done the exact same thing.

This one is actually true, baker. The text says the sailors dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for daybreak (Acts 27:29). They were afraid of running aground on the rocks. Nobody wants to find rocks in the dark, so they asked for morning.

The lifeboat, yes. The sailors were pretending to lower anchors from the bow, but what they let down into the sea was the lifeboat. That's the sneaky part, baker. They looked busy with the anchors while they were really trying to escape.

A fishing net would be a pretty strange move in the middle of the night during a storm, friend. The text says the sailors attempted to escape from the ship, and they let the lifeboat down into the sea. The anchors were just the cover story.

Close to the cover story, but not it. The sailors were only pretending to lower anchors from the bow. What they really let down into the sea was the lifeboat, and that's how you can tell they were trying to escape.

explanations.answer: If they leave you cannot be saved
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul told the centurion, the Roman officer in charge, and the soldiers, “Unless these men remain with the ship, you cannot be saved.” (Acts 27:31) He caught the plan and went straight to the people who could stop it. I think that's some quick thinking from a man who had been in a storm for two weeks.

explanations.answer: Let them go so the ship is lighter
explanations.explanation: Paul says the opposite of that. He told the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men remain with the ship, you cannot be saved.” (Acts 27:31) The sailors were needed on board, so Paul wanted them to stay, not go.

explanations.answer: Lock them below deck until morning
explanations.explanation: Locking them up sounds like a plan, friend, but that's not what Paul says. He tells the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men remain with the ship, you cannot be saved.” (Acts 27:31) The text has him warn them about the sailors, and then it moves to the lifeboat.

explanations.answer: Cut the ropes and let it drift
explanations.explanation: Snip, snip, and off it floats. Paul had just told the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men remain with the ship, you cannot be saved.” Then the soldiers cut the ropes to the lifeboat and set it adrift.

explanations.answer: Haul it back up on board
explanations.explanation: Hauling it back up makes sense, baker, but that's not what happened. The soldiers cut the ropes to the lifeboat and set it adrift. It floated off on the sea, and that was the end of the lifeboat.

explanations.answer: Tie it tight to the stern
explanations.explanation: Tying it tighter is the opposite of what these soldiers did, friend. They cut the ropes to the lifeboat and set it adrift. Cut ropes, not tied ones.

Eat is right. Right up to daybreak, Paul kept urging them all to eat. He told them, “Today is your fourteenth day in constant suspense, without taking any food.” (Acts 27:33) Fourteen days without food, and here's a man saying, come on, have something.

The sailors did pray earlier, for daybreak, but that's not what Paul urges here. The text says that right up to daybreak, Paul kept urging them all to eat. He pointed out that they had gone fourteen days without food. Then Paul gave thanks to God over the bread, so there's some prayer in there too.
Rest sounds lovely, baker. But Paul kept urging them all to eat. He told them it was their fourteenth day in constant suspense, without taking any food, and that it was for their own preservation.

True. Paul says, “…not a single hair of your head will be lost.” (Acts 27:34) He says it right after urging them to eat something for their own preservation. A promise like that is a lot to hand a hungry crew in a storm.

This one is true, friend. Paul told them, “…not a single hair of your head will be lost.” (Acts 27:34) He said it while urging them to eat for their own preservation. Hungry men on a battered ship got a promise along with that advice.

It goes the other way, baker. After Paul took bread, gave thanks to God in front of them all, broke it and began to eat, the text says, “They were all encouraged and took some food themselves.” (Acts 27:36) Nobody stayed too afraid to touch food.

False is right. The text says, “They were all encouraged and took some food themselves.” (Acts 27:36) They saw Paul give thanks to God over the bread and start eating. After that, the whole ship joined in.

explanations.answer: Throw the grain into the sea
explanations.explanation: Overboard goes the grain, baker. After the men had eaten their fill, they lightened the ship by throwing the grain into the sea. Eat first, then lighten the load, and that's the order the text gives.
The text never mentions cutting a sail loose, baker. It does say they hoisted the foresail to the wind when they made for the beach. To lighten the ship, it says they threw the grain into the sea.
Tossing the rudders isn't in the text, friend. It says they loosened the ropes that held the rudders, not that they threw them overboard. To lighten the ship, they threw the grain into the sea.

That's the plan. When daylight came, they did not recognize the land, but they sighted a bay with a sandy beach, where they decided to run the ship aground if they could. Notice the "…if they could." I think they were hoping it would work.
Waiting sounds calm, baker, but that's not what they did. They cut away the anchors and left them in the sea (Acts 27:40). The text says they decided to run the ship aground at the bay if they could.

Sailing past would have meant more time at sea, friend. They did not recognize the land, but they sighted a bay with a sandy beach and decided to run the ship aground there if they could. They headed straight for it.

Not quite, baker. The ship struck a sandbar and ran aground. The bow stuck fast and would not move, and the stern was being broken up by the pounding of the waves. So the ship did not make it all the way onto the beach.

False is right. The ship struck a sandbar and ran aground. The bow stuck fast and would not move, and the stern was being broken up by the pounding of the waves. They aimed for the beach, but a sandbar got in the way first.

Swim is right. The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners so none of them could swim to freedom. It's a heavy moment, so I'll say it plainly: this plan was a real threat to Paul and the others. Swimming turns out to matter again in the very next verses.

Sailing was off the table by then, baker. The ship was stuck on a sandbar and breaking up in the waves. The text says the soldiers planned to kill the prisoners so none of them could swim to freedom. It's a heavy part of the story.

Climbing is a fair guess with a ship coming apart, friend. But the text says the soldiers planned to kill the prisoners so none of them could swim to freedom. The danger was in the water, and it's a heavy moment in the story.

explanations.answer: He wants to spare Paul's life
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. The centurion, wanting to spare Paul's life, thwarted their plan. One officer stepped in and stopped it. I think Paul was glad he did.

explanations.answer: He needs every prisoner for trial
explanations.explanation: That sounds logical, baker, but the text doesn't say it. It says the centurion, wanting to spare Paul's life, thwarted the soldiers' plan. The reason is Paul, not a trial.

explanations.answer: He is afraid of the sailors
explanations.explanation: The text never says the centurion was afraid of the sailors, friend. It says the centurion, wanting to spare Paul's life, thwarted the soldiers' plan. The reason given is Paul.
True. The centurion commanded those who could swim to jump overboard first and get to land. I think that was a smart order. The rest were to follow after that.
This one is true, baker. The text says the centurion commanded those who could swim to jump overboard first and get to land. The rest were to follow after that.

explanations.answer: On planks and parts of the ship
explanations.explanation: Planks and parts of the ship, yes. The text says the rest were to follow on planks and various parts of the ship. Pieces of a ship that was breaking up became their way to land, and I'd have held on to mine with my mustache wrapped around it.
That lifeboat is long gone, baker. Back in Acts 27:32 the soldiers cut its ropes and set it adrift. The people who could not swim were told to follow on planks and various parts of the ship.
Walking would be nice, friend, but that's not what the text says. It says nothing about crossing the sandbar on foot. The rest were to follow on planks and various parts of the ship.

True. There were 276 on board, and the text says, “In this way everyone was brought safely to land.” (Acts 27:44) That's the same promise Paul made earlier about not losing a single hair (Acts 27:34). Every last one of them made it, baker.

This one is true, friend. The text counts 276 on board and then says, “In this way everyone was brought safely to land.” (Acts 27:44) Nobody was lost. That matches what Paul told them earlier, that not a single hair of their heads would be lost (Acts 27:34).
